analysis.one_liner: Bars dumping mine and other waste into rivers and streams as 'fill material.'
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 64 cosponsors to keep waste out of waterways died quietly in a House committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2002, federal regulators changed the definition of 'fill material' so that mining waste — including the leftover rock and dirt from mountaintop removal coal mining — could be dumped into streams and valleys as fill. H.R. 738 would have written into law that fill material can never be waste, closing that door. It won 64 cosponsors from both parties but never advanced past the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink from, fish in, or live near streams and rivers, especially communities in coal-mining regions where mountaintop-removal waste buries valley streams. The bill would also restore clearer legal limits for anyone who uses waterways downstream.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near streams and mining regions

how_it_helps.text: The bill defines fill material as anything that replaces waters of the United States with dry land or changes a water body's bottom elevation, and explicitly excludes any pollutant discharged 'primarily to dispose of waste' [S3] [S2].
That means waste could no longer qualify for the more permissive fill-dumping permits, so material like mine refuse could not simply be deposited into streams and valleys as 'fill' [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mining companies and other operations that dispose of waste in waterways would bear the cost of finding other disposal methods or treating waste, and some could face tighter limits on mountaintop-removal operations. Some legitimate construction and dredging fills would face stricter definitions as well.

drawbacks.text: Because the bill redefines fill 'for any purpose,' it could sweep in operations beyond waste dumping and complicate permitting for legitimate fills, such as infrastructure and dredged-material projects [S3].

Compliance costs would fall on mining and other industries that currently dispose of waste in waterways under the broader definition, and those costs could be passed to consumers or affect jobs in coal regions [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is clean water for downstream communities; the cost falls mainly on the industries that currently save money by dumping waste into streams. The bill is a narrow definitional fix — it does not ban fills generally, only waste disposed of as fill — so the main honest objection is that it could add friction to some legitimate fill permits.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its water subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 12, 2003, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and no further action appears in the record before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].
It attracted 64 cosponsors — 58 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but that support never translated into committee action or a floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining companies and other operations that dispose of waste in waterways are better off, because the 2002 rule allowing waste to be treated as fill stayed in effect and the statutory fix never advanced.

against.name: The 2002 EPA and Army Corps rule change
against.role: Regulators who redefined 'fill material' to include mine waste
against.what_they_did: Changed the federal definition of fill material so mining waste could be dumped into waterways, creating the loophole this bill sought to close; the executive branch had an interest in the bill not passing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was overwhelmingly Democratic (58 of 64 cosponsors), though a handful of Republicans including Christopher Shays joined at introduction; the committee that buried it was led by Republicans.

industries.note: These operators dispose of mine waste by dumping it into valley streams as 'fill' under the broader definition; the bill would have forced them to dispose of waste elsewhere, raising their costs. Their cost savings come at the expense of communities whose streams are buried and polluted.

industries.industry: Mining and industrial waste disposal generally
industries.note: Any operation discharging waste into waterways under the permissive fill rules would have lost that option, bearing the cost of alternative disposal or treatment.

The bill defines fill 'for any purpose,' so legitimate fills that change a water body's bottom elevation would fall under the new definition; most would still be permitted, but waste-based fills would no longer qualify.
